summary: Describes how to represent identity information in the RSVP POLICY_DATA object to support policy-based admission control, so a user and application can be securely identified.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP is the protocol a host uses to ask the network for a guaranteed quality of service on a data stream. The network checks policy before it grants the reservation, and the policy is usually about the user or the application making the request. This RFC defines how that identity travels in the RSVP message and how a router can check it.

questions: how does rsvp carry user identity
what is the rsvp policy locator
how does kerberos work with rsvp
subtitle: How RSVP messages carry a verifiable user or application identity so routers can apply policy to reservations.

tldr.problem: RSVP lets a host ask the network for a guaranteed quality of service, and the network checks policy before granting it. That policy is usually about the user or the application making the request, but the base RSVP specification has no way to carry an identity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an AUTH_DATA policy element inside the POLICY_DATA object, with a type number for user or application and a list of authentication attributes: a policy locator, a credential, a digital signature and a policy error object. Credentials can be a plain name, a Kerberos ticket or an X.509 certificate.
tldr.outcome: A router or policy decision point can authenticate the requester and apply policy to a named user or application. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2752 and corrects a P-Type codepoint and a field size error in it.

today: RFC 3182 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2001. It obsoletes RFC 2752, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why RSVP Needs an Identity
sections.content:
RSVP (RFC 2205) is a resource reservation setup protocol designed for an integrated services Internet. It is used by a host to request a specific quality of service from the network for particular application data streams or flows, and by routers to deliver QoS requests to all nodes along the path of the flows and to establish and maintain state to provide the requested service. RSVP requests generally result in resources being reserved in each node along the data path.

RSVP allows particular users to obtain preferential access to network resources under the control of an admission control mechanism. Permission to make a reservation is based both upon the availability of the requested resources along the path of the data and upon satisfaction of policy rules. Providing a policy-based admission control mechanism based on user identity or application is, the RFC says, one of the prime requirements. To solve these problems and implement identity-based policy control, it is required to identify the user or application making an RSVP request.

The document therefore proposes a mechanism for sending identification information in the RSVP messages, which enables authorization decisions based on policy and identity. It describes the authentication policy element, AUTH_DATA, contained in the POLICY_DATA object. A user process can generate an AUTH_DATA policy element and give it to the RSVP service on the originating host, and the RSVP service inserts it into the RSVP message to identify the owner, the user or application, making the request for network resources.

Network elements such as routers authenticate the request using the credentials presented in the AUTH_DATA and admit the RSVP message based on admission policy. After a request has been authenticated, the first hop router installs the RSVP state and forwards the new policy element returned by the Policy Decision Point described in RFC 2753. The RFC's abstract also records that it corrects an RSVP POLICY_DATA P-Type codepoint assignment error and a field size definition error in ErrorValue in RFC 2752.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP is the protocol a host uses to ask the network for a guaranteed quality of service on a data stream. The network checks policy before it grants the reservation, and the policy is usually about the user or the application making the request. This RFC defines how that identity travels in the RSVP message and how a router can check it.

sections.title: The AUTH_DATA Policy Element
sections.content:
POLICY_DATA objects contain policy information and are carried by RSVP messages; the format is described in "RSVP Extensions for Policy Control" (RFC 2750). The policy element defined here is the authentication data element, AUTH_DATA, which contains a list of authentication attributes.

The element has a Length, a P-Type and the attribute list. The Length is the length of the policy element, including the Length and P-Type fields, in octets, and it MUST be a multiple of 4; it indicates the end of the authentication attribute list. The P-Type, the Identity Type, is the type of identity information in the element, supplied as the policy element type. IANA acts as a registry for policy element types for identity, and initially the registry holds P-Type 2, AUTH_USER, an authentication scheme to identify users, and P-Type 3, AUTH_APP, an authentication scheme to identify applications.

Each authentication attribute carries information specific to the authentication method and the type of AUTH_DATA. The attribute is encoded as a multiple of 4 octets, and attributes that are not a multiple of 4 octets long MUST be padded to a 4-octet boundary. An attribute has a two-octet Length, a one-octet A-Type, a one-octet SubType and a Value. The Length indicates the actual length of the attribute, including the Length and A-Type fields, in octets, and does not include any padding bytes added to make the attribute a multiple of 4 octets long. The SubType depends on the A-Type.

IANA acts as a registry for A-Types, and initially the registry holds four. A-Type 1, POLICY_LOCATOR, is a unique string for locating the admission policy, such as an X.500 Distinguished Name. A-Type 2, CREDENTIAL, is a user credential such as a Kerberos ticket or a digital certificate, or an application credential such as an application ID. A-Type 3, DIGITAL_SIGNATURE, is a digital signature of the authentication data policy element. A-Type 4, POLICY_ERROR_OBJECT, carries detailed information on policy failures.

Each of the four has its own format. POLICY_LOCATOR holds an OctetString containing the Distinguished Name, and its SubType selects how that name is written: ASCII_DN, UNICODE_DN, ASCII_DN_ENCRYPT or UNICODE_DN_ENCRYPT. The two encrypted forms use the Kerberos session key or the digital certificate private key for encryption, and for Kerberos encryption the format is the same as returned from gss_seal in RFC 1509. The Length of a POLICY_LOCATOR attribute MUST be at least 4.

CREDENTIAL holds the credential itself. Its SubType values are ASCII_ID for a plain ASCII user or application identification, UNICODE_ID for the same in UNICODE, KERBEROS_TKT for a Kerberos ticket, X509_V3_CERT for an X.509 V3 digital certificate, and PGP_CERT for a PGP digital certificate. The Length of a CREDENTIAL attribute MUST be at least 4.

The DIGITAL_SIGNATURE attribute MUST be the last attribute in the list and holds the digital signature of the AUTH_DATA policy element, signing all the data in the element up to the DIGITAL_SIGNATURE. The algorithm used depends on the authentication method specified by the CREDENTIAL SubType. No sub-types are defined for it, so the SubType field MUST be set to 0, and its Length MUST be at least 4.

The POLICY_ERROR_CODE attribute is used to carry policy control errors generated by a node when processing or validating an authentication data policy element. When a policy node, whether a local policy decision point or a remote one, encounters a request that fails policy control due to its authentication policy element, it SHOULD add a POLICY_ERROR_CODE with more information about the reason into the policy element. That then causes an appropriate PATH_ERROR or RESV_ERROR message to be generated with the policy element and the appropriate RSVP error code, returned to the request's source. The AUTH_DATA policy element in a PATH or RESV message SHOULD NOT contain this attribute; it is inserted only into the error messages generated by policy-aware intermediate nodes. Its Length MUST be at least 8, its SubType MUST be set to 0, and its ErrorValue is a 16-bit code giving the reason the policy decision point failed to process the element.
sections.plainLanguage: The identity is carried in a policy element called AUTH_DATA inside the POLICY_DATA object of the RSVP message. It has a length, a type number saying whether it describes a user or an application, and a list of attributes. Each attribute has its own length, a type number and a sub-type number, followed by the value, and the whole thing is padded to a multiple of four bytes so that everything lines up.

sections.title: Four Ways to Fill It In
sections.content:
Section 4 of the RFC groups authentication attributes into a policy element to represent the identity credentials, and gives four concrete arrangements.

Simple user authentication encodes the user login ID, in plain ASCII or UNICODE text, as the CREDENTIAL attribute, alongside a POLICY_LOCATOR holding the user's Distinguished Name.

Kerberos user authentication uses Kerberos (RFC 1510), which uses a trusted third party, the Kerberos Distribution Center, to authenticate the user to a network server. It assumes a KDC is present and that both the host and the verifier of the authentication information, a router or a policy decision point, implement Kerberos. The CREDENTIAL attribute holds the Kerberos session ticket instead of a login ID.

The operational setting is described in Section 4.2.1. An RSVP-enabled host is configured to construct and insert an AUTH_DATA policy element into RSVP messages that designate the use of the Kerberos authentication method, KERBEROS_TKT. Upon RSVP session initialization the user application contacts the KDC to obtain a Kerberos ticket for the next network node or its policy decision point. A router generating an RSVP message contacts the KDC to obtain a Kerberos ticket for the next hop network node or its policy decision point. The identity of the policy decision point or next network hop can be statically configured, learned via DHCP or maintained in a directory service. The ticket is sent to the next network node in the RSVP message, and the KDC is used to validate the ticket and authenticate the user sending the message.

Public key based user authentication encodes a digital certificate as the user credential, and uses a digital signature to authenticate the user. It assumes that the RSVP service requestors have a pair of keys, a private key and a public key; that the private key is secured with the user; that the public keys are stored in digital certificates issued by a trusted party, the certificate authority; and that the verifier, a policy decision point or router, can verify the digital certificate. The requestor uses its private key to generate the DIGITAL_SIGNATURE, and the authenticators use the user's public key, stored in the digital certificate, to verify the signature and authenticate the user.

Simple application authentication encodes the application identification, such as an executable filename, as plain ASCII or UNICODE text, and uses P-Type AUTH_APP.
sections.plainLanguage: Four ways of filling it in are described. The simplest puts the login name in plain text. Kerberos puts a session ticket in. Public key puts a digital certificate and a signature in. And for an application, the identity can simply be the name of the program making the request.

sections.title: Who Generates What
sections.content:
Section 5 of the RFC shows a network of hosts and routers between two policy decision points, and then gives the rules for generating the policy elements.

Network nodes, hosts or routers, generate AUTH_DATA policy elements whose contents depend on the identity type used and the authentication method used. These generally contain authentication credentials, such as a Kerberos ticket or a digital certificate, and policy locators, which can be the X.500 Distinguished Name of the user or network node, or application names. A node generates the AUTH_DATA policy element containing the authentication identity when making the RSVP request or forwarding an RSVP message.

For a user AUTH_DATA policy element the rules are these. For unicast sessions the user policy locator is copied from the previous hop, and the authentication credentials are for the current network node identity. For multicast messages the user policy locator is for the current network node identity, and the authentication credentials are for the current network node.

For an application AUTH_DATA policy element the rules are these. For unicast sessions the application AUTH_DATA is copied from the previous hop. For multicast messages the application AUTH_DATA is either the first application AUTH_DATA in the message or chosen by the policy decision point.
sections.plainLanguage: Every node that forwards an RSVP message generates an AUTH_DATA element for itself. For a one-to-one session the user identity is copied from the previous hop but the credentials are for the current node. For a multicast session both are for the current node.

sections.title: Message Generation, Reception and Authentication
sections.content:
Section 6.1 covers message generation at the RSVP host. The RSVP message is created as specified in RFC 2205 with three modifications. The message MAY contain multiple AUTH_DATA policy elements. An authentication policy element is created and the IdentityType field is set to indicate the identity type in the policy element, with the Distinguished Name inserted as the POLICY_LOCATOR attribute and credentials such as a Kerberos ticket or digital certificate inserted as the CREDENTIAL attribute. The POLICY_DATA object containing the AUTH_DATA policy element is inserted in the RSVP message in the appropriate place, and if an INTEGRITY object is not computed for the RSVP message then an INTEGRITY object SHOULD be computed for the POLICY_DATA object, as described in RFC 2750, and inserted as a Policy Data option.

Section 6.2 covers message reception at the router, again with three modifications. If the router is not policy aware, it SHOULD send the RSVP message to the policy decision point and wait for a response; if the router is policy unaware, it ignores the policy data objects and continues processing the RSVP message. The message is rejected if the response from the policy decision point is negative. Processing of the RSVP message then continues.

Section 6.3 covers the authentication performed by the router or policy decision point. The AUTH_DATA policy element is retrieved, and the PE type field is checked, returning an error if the identity type is not supported. The user credential is then verified, in one of three ways. With simple authentication, the user ID is obtained and validated, or the executable name is obtained and validated. With Kerberos, the ticket is sent to the KDC to obtain the session key, and the session key is used to authenticate the user. With public key, the certificate is checked to see that it was issued by a trusted certificate authority, and the user or application is authenticated by verifying the digital signature.
sections.plainLanguage: The host builds the element and puts it in the RSVP message. A router that is not policy aware hands the message to the policy decision point and waits; a router that ignores policy data carries on without it. The verifier then checks the credentials, using the Kerberos key distribution centre, the certificate authority, or a simple name check.

sections.title: Error Signalling
sections.content:
If the policy decision point fails to verify the AUTH_DATA policy element, it MUST return a policy control failure, error code 02, to the policy enforcement point. The error values are described in RFC 2205 and RFC 2750. The policy decision point SHOULD also supply a policy data object containing an AUTH_DATA policy element with A-Type POLICY_ERROR_CODE giving more details on the failure, and the policy enforcement point will include that policy data object in the outgoing RSVP error message.

The five ErrorValues are the ones the RFC registers. ERROR_NO_MORE_INFO, value 1, means no information is available. UNSUPPORTED_CREDENTIAL_TYPE, value 2, means this type of credentials is not supported. INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES, value 3, means the credentials do not have sufficient privilege. EXPIRED_CREDENTIAL, value 4, means the credential has expired. IDENTITY_CHANGED, value 5, means the identity has changed.
sections.plainLanguage: When the check fails, the policy decision point returns a policy control failure and may add a short explanation, which the router passes back to the host in the error message. Five error values are defined, from no more information through to identity changed.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
Standard RSVP policy elements, the P-Type values, are assigned by IETF Consensus action as described in RFC 2750. P-Type AUTH_USER is assigned the value 2 and P-Type AUTH_APP the value 3.

Authentication attribute types, the A-Type values, in the range 0 to 127 are allocated through an IETF Consensus action, and A-Type values between 128 and 255 are reserved for private use and are not assigned by IANA. A-Type POLICY_LOCATOR is assigned the value 1, CREDENTIAL the value 2, DIGITAL_SIGNATURE the value 3 and POLICY_ERROR_OBJECT the value 4.

The same rule applies to the POLICY_LOCATOR SubType values: 0 to 127 by IETF Consensus action, 128 to 255 reserved for private use. POLICY_LOCATOR SubType ASCII_DN is assigned the value 1, UNICODE_DN the value 2, ASCII_DN_ENCRYPT the value 3 and UNICODE_DN_ENCRYPT the value 4.

The CREDENTIAL SubType values follow the same pattern. CREDENTIAL SubType ASCII_ID is assigned the value 1, UNICODE_ID the value 2, KERBEROS_TKT the value 3, X509_V3_CERT the value 4 and PGP_CERT the value 5.

ErrorValues in the range 0 to 32767 are allocated through an IETF Consensus action, and ErrorValues between 32768 and 65535 are reserved for private use and are not assigned by IANA. ERROR_NO_MORE_INFO is assigned the value 1, UNSUPPORTED_CREDENTIAL_TYPE the value 2, INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES the value 3, EXPIRED_CREDENTIAL the value 4 and IDENTITY_CHANGED the value 5.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA holds the registries for the type numbers, the attribute types and the error values, and the RFC lists the values assigned by this document. The ranges 128 to 255 of the attribute and sub-type registries are left for private use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The purpose of the memo is to describe a mechanism to authenticate RSVP requests based on user identity in a secure manner. The RSVP INTEGRITY object is used to protect the policy object containing the user identity information from security, replay, attacks. Combining the AUTH_DATA policy element and the INTEGRITY object results in a secure access control that enforces authentication based on both the identity of the user and the identity of the originating node.

The RFC then compares the three authentication methods. Simple authentication does not contain a credential that can be securely authenticated and is inherently less secured. The Kerberos authentication mechanism is reasonably well secured. User authentication using a public key certificate is known to provide the strongest security.
sections.plainLanguage: The RSVP INTEGRITY object protects the policy object holding the identity, so a captured message cannot be replayed. Combining it with AUTH_DATA gives an access control that checks both the user and the node that sent the request. The RFC ranks the three methods: a plain name is the weakest, Kerberos is reasonably well secured, and a public key certificate is the strongest.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the policy element in octets; must be a multiple of 4.

fields.name: P-Type
fields.desc: Identity type: 2 for AUTH_USER, 3 for AUTH_APP.

fields.name: Authentication Attribute List
fields.desc: The attributes, each padded to a 4-octet boundary.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the attribute in octets, excluding padding.

fields.name: A-Type
fields.desc: Attribute type: 1 POLICY_LOCATOR, 2 CREDENTIAL, 3 DIGITAL_SIGNATURE, 4 POLICY_ERROR_OBJECT.

fields.name: SubType
fields.desc: Meaning depends on the A-Type; 0 where no sub-type is defined.

items.label: POLICY_LOCATOR
items.desc: A unique string locating the admission policy, such as an X.500 Distinguished Name.

items.label: CREDENTIAL
items.desc: A user credential such as a Kerberos ticket or digital certificate, or an application ID.

items.label: DIGITAL_SIGNATURE
items.desc: Signature of the AUTH_DATA element; must be the last attribute in the list.

items.label: ASCII_ID
items.desc: User or application identification in plain ASCII text.

items.label: UNICODE_ID
items.desc: User or application identification in UNICODE text.

items.label: UNSUPPORTED_CREDENTIAL_TYPE
items.desc: This type of credentials is not supported.

items.label: INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES
items.desc: The credentials do not have sufficient privilege.
